# Australia needs to stand up to # Trump # US presidential # intervention in # markets that added one trillion dollars to the value of a company. New US # tariffs being announced, even as negotiations were underway on a completely different set of tariffs. Even by # Trump 's standards, the US president's actions this week have seen global politics, economics, markets and technology all disrupting each other and producing a new level of # chaos in unprecedented ways. South-east Asian countries alone were trying to come to terms with the impact of Trump interventions that will hinder their push into # DataCentres and limit their capacity to buy # Nvidia chips, only to discover that the US was also proposing new tariffs on many of those countries on other goods. There are billions of dollars of data centre projects under construction in the region, partly because # Chinese companies 'rent out' access to Nvidia chips in third countries. The economic shiver going through countries like # Indonesia , # Singapore , # Thailand and # Malaysia is significant. By contrast, the collapse of global # ClimateChange talks — co-chaired by Australia and at which the US was not present — had at least been predictable. And this chaos followed a week in which # China had very ostentatiously signalled its arrival at the centre of world power in # Shenzen , promoting itself as a bastion of calm and steady power. It's hard to think of a better time for what was promoted as a "major" and "landmark" foreign policy speech to the Senate from Foreign Minister # PennyWong . For much of this year, the global economy has been reeling from the effects of Trump's and # Israel 's # BenjaminNetanyahu 's war on Iran. But it seems the US president doesn't even need that # war to create # chaos for the rest of us. Consider the details of some of his actions this week. Trump has essentially forced a public company to reinstate an executive whose private life is seen by US # IntelligenceAgencies as a # NationalSecurity risk, and who faces questioning from federal and state authorities, as well as # Congress . Pfft! said the president. He's a good guy. The shock announcement on Tuesday morning (Australian time) that # JensenHuang would be returning to Nvidia after # WhiteHouse pressure sent the US markets surging. That seemed to be the aim, given so much of the markets and the US economy are now bound up in the # AI boom. Yet, at the same time, the Trump administration was putting in place a series of measures trying to control the entire Nvidia market not just in China, but in other countries too. Like many Trump initiatives, the market surge didn't last. By Friday, most of it had disappeared as investors refocused on the whole spectre of the # AIBubble bursting, and other uncertainties, including continued disruption to # oil supplies and # trade caused by the US president. The rest of the world has become somewhat more forthright about criticising Trump's actions. China, the # EU and # India were quite clear, for example, on their views about his latest tariff move. But in Australia, it seems we just can't do it. The problem is not that Senator Wong used her speech this week to defend the # alliance , or # AUKUS . It was more in the silences about broader world trends where the speech just reeked of an inability to call a spade a spade when it comes to the # UnitedStates . This meekness isn't just a political issue: the latest Lowy Institute poll of analysts, released this week, gives marks to the government for its non-confrontational style. The foreign minister's speech set out six shifts in the international system. Wong identified a growing and more frequent use of force and coercion and that the great powers have fundamentally shifted how they define and pursue their interests. She mentioned that trade investment and technology have lifted living standards; that technology is transforming the foundations and the dimensions of economic and strategic power; and that it is more challenging for countries to exercise power together. So what examples does she give of "the growing and more frequent use of force and coercion"? The speech names # Russia , # NorthKorea and China. The United States doesn't get a mention, despite # Venezuela , despite # Greenland , despite # Canada , despite # Cuba , and despite pressure and threats to # Colombia and # Honduras . The speech criticises the US only in the abstract plural, and every concrete example of bad behaviour is an adversary. Wong only put China and the US side-by-side once, when she says that the "great powers — the United States and China — are competing … with less regard for the guardrails". When the speech speaks of economic coercion it lists "concentrated supply chains, control of essential resources and restrictions on access to markets" — which all have a distinct China feel to them. # UStariffs , including on Australia, go unmentioned. The United States, the foreign minister says, is "changing its priorities". It is "a vigorous democracy with the ability to remake and reimagine itself"; a country that "has never stood still". Perhaps the most striking thing is that while the speech says that "wars in … the # MiddleEast have upended the world's energy and commodity markets", it neglects to mention who might have started the war. The only time the speech names the US - # Iran conflict, it is through the topic of # Iranian disinformation, not as a war Australia backed. Analysts who are critical of the government's approach don't argue that we should walk away from # America , just be a bit less mincing about how we talk about the place. Yet, this week's speech illustrates just how entrenched the twee language — even the thinking about our "great ally" — really is. Penny Wong has always argued for a quiet, steady, cautious approach to diplomacy. And she would argue the improvements in our relationships with the Pacific, around our region, and with China are all endorsements of this. But the government also likes to present itself as being a torch bearer for Australia's long history as a "middle power". It's a history that saw it have a central role in the establishment of the post-WWII international order, as well as more recent initiatives, from nuclear non-proliferation, to peace in Cambodia, and the end of the apartheid regime in # SouthAfrica . A changing role for the middle powers has been at the centre of the shifts in the international system we have seen this year, as the US has increasingly gone rogue. The poster boy for that move has been Canada's # MarkCarney . And it feels like Australia is leaving him to run the race on calling out the United States. Prime Minister Anthony # Albanese agreed with the major speech Carney gave at the beginning of the year, which lit this issue up, and subsequently invited him to Australia. In practical terms, the relationship between our two countries has had its biggest upgrade in a generation, including on our biggest ever defence export deal to provide Canada with the over-the-horizon radar system. The decline in power and coherent strategy from the US gives Australia not just the opportunity, not just the excuse, but an interest in regaining a more assertive voice in international affairs.
